paragraphs: The paper studies clustering when each data point has several different views, each sufficient to support clustering on its own. Instead of treating those views as unrelated tasks, it proposes a spectral clustering algorithm that lets them inform a shared grouping. The approach draws on co-training, an idea usually associated with semi-supervised learning.

Its central assumption is that the underlying cluster membership should remain the same whichever view is used. The algorithm therefore restricts its search to clusterings that agree across views. This agreement requirement gives the multiple representations a concrete role: a proposed grouping must be compatible with more than one account of the data. Its justification depends on the stated shared-clustering assumption.

The authors also emphasize that their algorithm introduces no hyperparameters to set, making it attractive in an unsupervised setting where tuning can be difficult. Comparisons with baseline methods on synthetic and real-world datasets support its effectiveness. These results provide empirical evidence for using cross-view agreement to guide spectral clustering.
icml-2011-a-co-training-approach-for-mul.tldr: A hyperparameter-free spectral clustering method combines multiple views by searching for clusterings that agree across them.

paragraphs: The paper addresses approximate maximum a posteriori inference on factor graphs: finding a high-scoring joint assignment while respecting the relationships and constraints represented by the graph. Its proposed algorithm combines dual decomposition, which divides the inference problem into smaller subproblems, with augmented Lagrangian optimization to coordinate their solutions.

Each subproblem receives a quadratic penalty that encourages agreement with the others. This matters because solving the pieces independently is insufficient when they make conflicting choices about shared variables. The penalty is intended to drive consensus faster than earlier approaches based on subgradients. The algorithm is parallelizable and supports fine decompositions, allowing the graph to be divided into many small pieces.

The authors establish convergence and describe how simple sorting operations can efficiently accommodate structural constraints, including constraints that may span the whole problem. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data compare favorably with competing methods. The convergence result concerns the proposed approximate inference algorithm; the abstract does not equate convergence with exact MAP recovery.
icml-2011-an-augmented-lagrangian-approa.tldr: Quadratic agreement penalties make decomposed approximate MAP inference convergent, parallelizable, and able to handle structural constraints efficiently.

paragraphs: Many inference tasks in graphical models require adding contributions from possible assignments of variables. Computing a partition function or the probability of observed evidence are two examples. The paper develops an approximate inference algorithm that supplies both upper and lower bounds on such sums, giving information about their possible values rather than only a single estimate.

The mathematical foundation is Holder's inequality. The resulting framework connects approaches that otherwise look quite different: variable elimination techniques, including mini-bucket elimination, and variational techniques, including tree reweighted belief propagation and conditional entropy decomposition. The contribution is both a unification of these existing ideas and an extension beyond them.

The authors report that combining benefits from these approaches yields significantly better bounds on sum-product tasks. Tighter bounds matter because they constrain the target quantity more closely, improving the information available from approximate inference. The stated advance is therefore about the quality of bounded calculations and a shared framework for obtaining them, rather than a claim that these summation problems become exactly solvable.
icml-2011-bounding-the-partition-functio.tldr: An inference algorithm based on Holder's inequality unifies elimination and variational methods to obtain better upper and lower bounds on graphical-model sums.

paragraphs: Graph embedding represents graph nodes as points in a lower-dimensional space. When edge weights encode similarity, a useful representation should place strongly similar objects near one another. The paper questions whether Laplacian embedding preserves these local relationships as reliably as is often assumed, showing that it frequently falls short of that expectation.

The authors propose Cauchy graph embedding with a new objective aimed at preserving the original similarity relationships in the embedded space. The focus is on the usefulness of local neighborhoods after dimensionality reduction. If the embedding changes which objects appear close together, methods that depend on nearby examples can receive a misleading representation of the original data.

The paper reports that the proposed embedding supports better performance on downstream tasks such as nearest-neighbor classification. Experiments on synthetic data and real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate its usefulness. These findings support changing the embedding objective to better retain local similarity, while the criticism of Laplacian embedding is that it often fails to preserve topology well, not that it always fails.
icml-2011-cauchy-graph-embedding-555215b.tldr: Cauchy graph embedding uses a new objective to better preserve local similarities and improve tasks performed on the resulting representation.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the challenge of converting data into short codes that still support accurate nearest-neighbor search in massive databases. Its motivation is that meaningful neighborhoods may follow a low-dimensional manifold within the data. A compact code should therefore reflect the data's neighborhood structure, rather than merely compress each point independently.

The proposed method learns codes from a graph that captures those relationships. To make this feasible computationally, it uses Anchor Graphs to construct tractable low-rank adjacency matrices. It also extends graph Laplacian eigenvectors into eigenfunctions, allowing a newly encountered point to be hashed in constant time under the formulation.

A hierarchical threshold-learning procedure extracts multiple bits from each eigenfunction, which the authors report improves search accuracy. Comparisons with other leading methods on two large datasets support the overall approach. The paper thus connects neighborhood discovery, manageable graph computation, and efficient encoding of new points. The constant-time claim applies to hashing a new point, rather than to the entire learning or search process.
icml-2011-hashing-with-graphs-23127677bd.tldr: Graph-based hashing learns compact codes that preserve neighborhood structure while supporting constant-time encoding of new data points.

paragraphs: Regularization usually changes an optimization objective to favor solutions that remain useful despite noisy data. Solving the modified problem can add computational cost. This paper investigates a different possibility: computational shortcuts may already impose a form of regularization, even when no explicit regularization term appears in the original calculation.

The authors study approximations to the smallest nontrivial eigenvector of a graph Laplacian. They analyze three procedures based on random walks: a graph heat-kernel method, a PageRank-based method, and a truncated lazy random walk. For each procedure, they ask which regularized optimization problem its output can be understood as solving exactly.

The contribution is a precise characterization of that implicit regularization for all three procedures. A crucial distinction is that the corresponding regularization acts on a related semidefinite program, rather than on the usual vector formulation of the eigenvector problem. This gives a mathematical interpretation to the shortcuts: their approximations can also be viewed as exact solutions to particular regularized problems.
icml-2011-implementing-regularization-im.tldr: Three random-walk methods for approximate eigenvector computation are characterized as exactly solving related regularized semidefinite problems.

paragraphs: Fisher kernels turn structured objects into vector representations using a generative model. The paper investigates how class labels can improve those representations themselves. Its goal is to make the vectors reflect distinctions relevant to classification, so that the representation carries useful label information before a classifier is trained on it.

The method draws on metric learning and changes how the generative model is trained. Each object's representation involves gradients of its log-likelihood. Training seeks to bring these gradient vectors closer together for objects with the same label and move them farther apart for objects with different labels. Labels therefore influence the geometry induced by the model, rather than only the classifier that uses its output.

The authors illustrate strong classifier performance using the learned representations in handwriting recognition, speech recognition, facial expression analysis, and bioinformatics. These applications demonstrate the approach across several kinds of structured objects. The central contribution is a way to train a generative representation with a discriminative purpose: organize its gradient features around the categories that the eventual prediction task must distinguish.
icml-2011-learning-discriminative-fisher.tldr: Label-guided training makes Fisher-kernel representations bring same-class objects together and separate objects from different classes.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn distributions over preferences when the available evidence consists of pairwise comparisons. Such comparisons express a preference between two items without requiring a complete ranking. The authors relax restrictive assumptions made by earlier learning methods and present what they identify as the first algorithms for learning Mallows models and their mixtures from this evidence.

The core tool is the generalized repeated insertion model, or GRIM, an algorithm for sampling from arbitrary ranking distributions. The authors develop approximate samplers that become exact in many important special cases and provide provable bounds when pairwise evidence is present. This distinction matters: exactness is established for particular cases, rather than for every sampling problem the approach can address.

The sampling machinery supports algorithms for evaluating log-likelihood, learning mixtures of Mallows models, and nonparametric estimation. Experiments on large real-world datasets demonstrate effectiveness. The broader contribution is to make pairwise preference evidence usable in a collection of probabilistic learning operations, connecting basic comparisons to richer models of rankings.
icml-2011-learning-mallows-models-with-p.tldr: New sampling and learning algorithms fit Mallows preference models and mixtures from arbitrary pairwise comparisons.

paragraphs: The paper addresses training recurrent neural networks on difficult sequences, especially when useful information must persist across long stretches of data. It attributes substantial importance to the optimization procedure and combines advances in Hessian-free optimization with a new damping scheme to make training effective on challenging sequence-modeling problems.

The evaluation covers two distinct settings. One consists of synthetic datasets with extremely long-term dependencies that the abstract describes as impossible for standard optimization approaches. The other consists of three complex real-world sequence datasets. Successful training in the synthetic setting demonstrates the method's ability to handle the particular long-dependency challenges represented by those problems.

On the three real-world datasets, the authors report significant improvements over the Long Short-term Memory approach used as the previous leading method for training neural sequence models. This is an empirical comparison on those tasks, rather than a universal ranking of architectures. The paper also offers a new interpretation of the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix used within Hessian-free optimization, contributing understanding of a mathematical component behind the training method.
icml-2011-learning-recurrent-neural-netw.tldr: Hessian-free optimization with a new damping scheme trains RNNs on difficult long-dependency tasks and outperforms LSTM on three reported real-world datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear regression when the model's parameter is a matrix whose rank must remain fixed. This requirement constrains the set of allowable regression models. The authors approach the problem by studying the geometry of that set, treating fixed-rank matrices as a Riemannian manifold on which optimization can be performed.

Using this geometric view, they develop efficient line-search algorithms. The rank restriction becomes part of the space being searched, giving a principled basis for designing updates within the constrained problem. The approach also provides a geometric interpretation of recent work on learning fixed-rank matrices, connecting algorithm design to the structure of the parameter space.

The proposed methods scale to high-dimensional problems and have local convergence properties. That qualification places the convergence claim near a solution rather than asserting guaranteed discovery of a global optimum. Benchmark experiments suggest performance competitive with leading alternatives. Together, the geometry and numerical results support manifold optimization as a versatile framework for constructing machine-learning algorithms with fixed-rank constraints.
icml-2011-linear-regression-under-fixed-.tldr: Riemannian geometry yields efficient line-search algorithms for fixed-rank linear regression with local convergence properties and competitive benchmark results.

paragraphs: Linear support vector machines are appealing for large datasets because they are simple and fast to apply, but a single linear boundary cannot separate every classification problem. Kernel SVMs address nonlinear structure at a computational and memory cost. Their predictions depend on support vectors, whose number has been observed experimentally to grow with training-set size.

The paper proposes a locally linear SVM with a smooth decision boundary and bounded curvature. Local codings approximate the functions defining the classifier, allowing the model to represent nonlinear decisions through local linear structure. The authors also show how to train it online using stochastic gradient descent, with the same convergence guarantees as the standard gradient-descent method for linear SVMs.

The reported results combine classification performance comparable to leading methods with substantially faster operation than competing kernel SVMs. This makes the contribution a practical attempt to retain useful nonlinear behavior while reducing the cost associated with kernel classifiers. The paper also generalizes the construction to locally finite-dimensional kernel SVMs.
icml-2011-locally-linear-support-vector-.tldr: Locally linear SVMs provide smooth nonlinear decision boundaries with online training and reported speed advantages over competing kernel SVMs.

paragraphs: Stochastic learning methods often use approximate subgradient steps to handle large datasets or streaming observations. When their objective includes a nonsmooth regularizer, that term can encourage a structured solution, such as a sparse one. The paper examines how an optimization algorithm can recognize the lower-dimensional structure that the regularizer is trying to produce.

The key observation is that a solution often lies on a low-dimensional manifold where the otherwise nonsmooth regularizer becomes smooth. The authors show that regularized dual averaging can identify this manifold with high probability. Identifying it means learning a useful restriction on where to search, in addition to making progress toward a good objective value.

This result motivates a two-stage strategy. Once a near-optimal manifold has been identified, optimization switches to a method that searches only within it. Because this space typically has much lower intrinsic dimension, the restricted search can converge quickly to a near-optimal point with the intended structure. Computational results illustrate these claims, while the identification guarantee remains probabilistic.
icml-2011-manifold-identification-of-dua.tldr: Regularized dual averaging can identify a solution's low-dimensional manifold with high probability, motivating faster optimization restricted to that structure.

paragraphs: The paper studies finite-horizon Markov decision processes where performance depends on both the average cumulative reward and its variance. Considering variance changes the objective: two policies with similar expected rewards may differ in how variable their outcomes are. One problem examined is maximizing expected reward while imposing a constraint on that variability.

The authors show that randomizing decisions or using the history of the process can improve performance. These are possibility results: they establish that such policy choices can matter, without claiming that every problem requires them. The findings make the policy class part of the optimization issue, because restricting how decisions are made can exclude better mean-variance tradeoffs.

The paper also establishes computational difficulty. Finding a policy that maximizes the mean under a variance constraint is NP-hard in some cases and strongly NP-hard in others. Alongside these hardness results, the authors offer pseudo-polynomial exact algorithms and approximation algorithms. The contribution therefore combines an account of useful policy flexibility with complexity results and algorithmic approaches.
icml-2011-mean-variance-optimization-in-.tldr: Mean-variance objectives can benefit from randomized or history-based policies, but optimizing them is computationally hard in the cases analyzed.

paragraphs: Fully Bayesian estimation for probabilistic PCA is computationally intractable, motivating approximations. The paper compares partially Bayesian PCA, which integrates out latent variables, with variational Bayesian PCA, which also integrates out loading vectors. It asks whether the variational approach is preferable for computational efficiency and automatic selection of the representation's dimensionality.

The authors show that automatic dimensionality selection is available in partially Bayesian PCA as well. Its global solution can also be computed analytically, giving it a computational advantage. However, they establish an important drawback: in the empirical Bayesian framework, partially Bayesian PCA produces a trivial solution. Its analytical convenience therefore does not settle the practical comparison.

The paper then examines a simplified variational formulation with stronger independence assumptions between latent variables and loading vectors than ordinary variational Bayesian PCA. Its global optimum has an efficiently computable closed form. Experiments show that its empirical Bayes solution performs as well as the original variational approach, supporting the authors' conclusion that this simplified formulation offers the most advantageous practical combination among the approaches considered.
icml-2011-on-bayesian-pca-automatic-dime.tldr: A simplified variational Bayesian PCA admits an efficient closed-form optimum and experimentally matches the original formulation's empirical Bayes performance.

paragraphs: The paper examines the choice of optimizer for deep learning. Although stochastic gradient descent is straightforward to implement, the authors identify tuning and parallelization as obstacles to developing and scaling models. They investigate whether established optimization methods can simplify training while making better use of available computation.

Their experiments use limited-memory BFGS and conjugate gradient with line search. The authors find that these methods can substantially simplify and accelerate pretraining. The differences from stochastic gradient methods become more pronounced when training includes extensions such as sparsity regularization or uses hardware such as GPUs and computer clusters.

Distributed optimization experiments support using L-BFGS with locally connected and convolutional networks. The paper also reports a 0.69% result on MNIST for a convolutional model trained with L-BFGS, describing it as state of the art among methods using neither distortions nor pretraining. That comparison has a specific scope. Overall, the experiments support taking optimizer choice seriously when assessing training speed, implementation demands, and opportunities for parallel computation.
icml-2011-on-optimization-methods-for-de.tldr: Experiments show that L-BFGS and conjugate gradient can simplify and speed deep-learning pretraining, especially with regularization or parallel hardware.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a nonparametric Bayesian model that brings dictionary learning and topic modeling into a single framework. Its application is the analysis of partially annotated images. This setting combines visual observations with incomplete descriptive information, making the relationship between image representation and topic structure central to the modeling task.

Dictionary learning operates directly on image patches. This places the visual representation component at the level of local image content, while topic modeling forms another part of the same probabilistic model. The contribution is the joint formulation: the two modeling ideas are integrated rather than presented as separate analyses of the images. The Bayesian framework supplies the common setting in which they are combined.

For inference, the authors use a Gibbs-slice sampler and describe the procedure as efficient. They report encouraging results on widely used datasets. Those findings support the promise of combining patch-based dictionary learning with topic modeling for partially annotated images. The abstract's empirical claim is encouraging performance, without a stronger claim of universal superiority or a quantified improvement.
icml-2011-on-the-integration-of-topic-mo.tldr: A nonparametric Bayesian framework integrates patch-based dictionary learning and topic modeling to analyze partially annotated images.

paragraphs: Bernoulli-logistic latent Gaussian models combine binary observations with underlying Gaussian variables. Estimating their parameters is difficult because the marginal likelihood requires an intractable logistic-Gaussian integral. The paper addresses that bottleneck by replacing a troublesome function within the calculation with fixed upper bounds made from linear or quadratic pieces.

These bounds target the logistic-log-partition function. The authors develop a framework for approximately finding minimax-optimal piecewise quadratic bounds, seeking to control the largest approximation error across the function. They also construct a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm that uses the piecewise bounds to estimate model parameters.

A theoretical result links the maximum error of the function bound to the maximum error in the marginal-likelihood estimate. This connection explains why improving the local approximation is relevant to the quantity needed for learning. Empirical results show that piecewise bounds can be significantly more accurate than previously proposed variational bounds. The contribution combines a practical estimation procedure with an explicit relationship between approximation quality and likelihood-estimation error.
icml-2011-piecewise-bounds-for-estimatin.tldr: Piecewise function bounds enable approximate estimation of logistic latent Gaussian models, with error guarantees and reported accuracy gains over earlier variational bounds.

paragraphs: In network classification, obtaining a node's label can help in two different ways. It can improve the learned model, and it can directly improve predictions as label information propagates through the network. The paper argues that evaluating both effects together can obscure whether an active-learning strategy actually learns a better model.

The authors use classification across networks to separate learning improvements from prediction improvements and focus on reducing learning error. When label propagation is part of learning, they find that choosing nodes whose predictions are more certain is more effective than choosing uncertain nodes. This conclusion is tied to that learning setting, rather than a general rejection of uncertainty-based active learning.

They propose a method combining a network-based certainty measure, semi-supervised learning, and relational resampling. Experiments on synthetic and real-world networks show faster learning than several baselines. The main implication is that label selection should be judged against the intended benefit: improving a transferable model can favor different queries from those that immediately improve collective predictions within one network.
icml-2011-relational-active-learning-for.tldr: When label propagation supports learning, certainty-based network queries can improve model learning more effectively than uncertainty-based queries.

paragraphs: The paper studies minimizing a submodular function when the chosen set must satisfy a size constraint. Without constraints, submodular minimization has strongly polynomial algorithms. Adding a size requirement changes the computational picture: the problem is NP-hard and includes the densest subgraph and uniform graph partitioning problems as special cases.

Rather than approximating an optimum for any requested size, the proposed algorithm computes exact optimal solutions for some of the possible size constraints. This is the central distinction in its guarantee. It does not promise to solve the problem optimally for an arbitrary size supplied in advance, which is precisely where the general computational difficulty remains.

The method uses the polyhedral theory associated with submodular functions and runs in polynomial time for its stated task. Computational experiments evaluate its performance. The contribution identifies a way to obtain exact answers within a difficult constrained problem by changing which size constraints the algorithm resolves, rather than weakening the quality of the solutions returned through an approximation guarantee.
icml-2011-size-constrained-submodular-mi.tldr: A polynomial-time algorithm finds exact submodular minima for some size constraints, without claiming to solve every prescribed size.

paragraphs: The paper proposes learning a kernel-based regression function by adapting the kernel combination to the prediction task. Its building blocks are parameterized kernels based on the data. These are assembled through conical combinations, meaning combinations with nonnegative weights, so the resulting kernel construction is itself part of what is learned.

To carry out this learning, the authors introduce a stochastic convex optimization procedure and establish convergence guarantees. They emphasize that its individual updates are inexpensive. This connects two aspects of the method: the flexibility to learn a task-specific kernel combination and an optimization strategy intended to keep the repeated learning steps computationally manageable.

The authors present experiments on several benchmark datasets to assess the suitability of the strategy. The stated contribution rests on automatic adaptation to the regression task, inexpensive updates, and convergence analysis. These properties address different concerns: adaptation determines what model is learned, update cost affects the work needed to train it, and convergence theory supports the behavior of the proposed optimization procedure.
icml-2011-stochastic-low-rank-kernel-lea.tldr: A stochastic convex method learns task-adapted nonnegative kernel combinations for regression using inexpensive updates with convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the infinite regionalized policy representation for reinforcement learning in partially observable Markov decision processes. In this setting, the learner must make decisions without directly observing the complete underlying state. The proposed policy representation is nonparametric: its number of decision states is inferred from experience rather than fixed beforehand.

The model assumes an unbounded collection of possible decision states a priori. This does not mean that every learned policy must use infinitely many states. Instead, the representation leaves the number open and learns how many are needed to express the policy from the experiences available. Policy complexity therefore becomes part of the learning problem.

The authors propose algorithms that learn the number of decision states while maintaining a balance between exploration and exploitation. This couples representation learning with the choice of how to gather and use experience. They provide convergence analysis and evaluations on benchmark problems. The contribution is an adaptive policy representation together with learning algorithms and supporting analysis, rather than simply a fixed policy structure with adjustable parameters.
icml-2011-the-infinite-regionalized-poli.tldr: A nonparametric policy representation learns its number of decision states from experience while balancing exploration and exploitation.

paragraphs: The paper studies grouping time series, motivated by the effort required to label large motion-capture collections manually. Its aim is to cluster sequences while learning their joint temporal dynamics, accommodating time lags, and producing interpretable features. These requirements make the evolution of a sequence central to how it is represented.

The proposed model uses complex-valued linear dynamical systems, with real-valued Kalman filters included as a special case. The complex-valued formulation allows a diagonal transition matrix and a transmission matrix that the authors describe as easier to interpret. The title's claim of simplicity refers to this simpler model structure despite the use of complex-valued quantities.

The authors introduce Complex-Fit, an expectation-maximization algorithm for learning both the general model and its clustering special case. On real motion-capture sequences, they report clustering quality between 1.5 and 5 times better than well-known competitors. These results support the approach on the evaluated sequences and connect the proposed representation's temporal modeling capabilities to improved empirical clustering.
icml-2011-time-series-clustering-complex.tldr: Complex-valued dynamical systems simplify temporal modeling and yield reported clustering-quality gains on real motion-capture sequences.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning aims to improve prediction by supplementing limited labeled examples with unlabeled data. The paper begins from a practical problem: using those extra examples can sometimes make performance worse than learning only from the labels. It focuses on reducing this risk for semi-supervised support vector machines.

The proposed S4VM approach considers multiple candidate low-density separators simultaneously. Conventional semi-supervised SVMs typically seek a single optimal separator in a low-density region. Considering several candidates is intended to reduce the chance that unlabeled data steers learning toward a poor choice. The authors describe two implementations of this strategy.

Across their experiments, S4VMs achieve overall performance highly competitive with semi-supervised SVMs while never being significantly inferior to inductive SVMs. The latter comparison is the evidence for the method's safety motivation: the supervised alternative provides the reference point for avoiding harm. The reported finding is empirical and qualified by significance; it does not establish that unlabeled data can never reduce performance on any possible dataset.
icml-2011-towards-making-unlabeled-data-.tldr: S4VMs consider multiple separators to reduce harm from unlabeled data and are never significantly worse than supervised SVMs in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Standard Gaussian-process regression assumes that observation noise has the same magnitude throughout the input space. The paper addresses situations where that assumption is too restrictive because noise changes with the input. Modeling this variation produces a heteroscedastic Gaussian process, but makes inference harder than in the constant-noise formulation.

The authors introduce a nonstandard variational approximation that permits accurate inference with input-dependent noise. Its computational cost is roughly twice that of a standard Gaussian process, while retaining cubic scaling in the number of observations. This offers a quantified tradeoff: a more flexible noise model at a higher computational cost, without changing the stated scaling order.

Accuracy is assessed through comparison with Markov chain Monte Carlo, used as a reference for inference quality. Experiments on varied synthetic and real datasets illustrate effectiveness, and the paper also considers volatility forecasting. The contribution is a practical approximate-inference method that lets the model account for changing observation noise while keeping its computational requirements closely related to those of standard Gaussian-process regression.
icml-2011-variational-heteroscedastic-ga.tldr: A variational approximation enables accurate Gaussian-process regression with input-dependent noise at roughly twice the standard computational cost.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning relationships between structured inputs and structured outputs using both labeled and unlabeled examples. Its goal is to use two forms of structure together: the geometry of the input data and dependencies among output components. This extends manifold regularization beyond predictions represented by a single scalar.

The formulation uses vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and assumes that the output space has a Hilbert-space structure. Its regularization encourages predictions to vary smoothly with input geometry while also accounting for relationships within the output. These are complementary sources of information: nearby inputs constrain prediction behavior, and related outputs inform how the prediction components fit together.

The authors propose matrix-valued kernels that permit efficient implementation through numerical solvers for Sylvester matrix equations. Experiments on multilabel image annotation and text classification compare favorably with several alternatives. The contribution is therefore both a structured extension of manifold regularization and a computational route for applying it, with empirical support in tasks where several output labels must be considered.
icml-2011-vector-valued-manifold-regular.tldr: Vector-valued manifold regularization combines input geometry and output dependencies for learning from labeled and unlabeled data.
